title: Kant's Groundwork grounds morality in duty
body: Immanuel Kant's Groundwork of the Metaphysics of Morals is the short book in which he argues that moral obligation comes from reason. The text is on Wikisource. The Stanford Encyclopedia entry "Kant's Moral Philosophy" is a guide to the arguments. The central idea is the categorical imperative: a reason for acting that holds only because you want some result is hypothetical, and a reason that holds regardless of what you want is categorical. Moral worth, on this account, depends on acting from duty, not only on doing what duty would have required while aiming at something else. The view is a proposal in moral philosophy. It is not an empirical finding that people in fact act this way. Consequentialist theories deny that the right act is fixed independently of outcomes. That disagreement is still live.

contested_views.position: The moral law is a categorical demand of reason, and the worth of an act depends on acting from duty.
The right act is fixed by the goodness of outcomes.
contested_views.held_by: Consequentialist theories, as surveyed in the Stanford Encyclopedia
